# When a Description Becomes a Verdict

*Expertise, explanation, and the scope of judgment*

## 1. The extra conclusion

A proof is described as technical. An exposition begins with elementary material. A theory reformulates something already known. These can be useful descriptions. Sometimes even “merely” is warranted: a claimed innovation really is a standard construction once its notation has been unpacked.

The difficulty begins when the description is asked to settle a further question. Familiar ingredients are treated as settling what their arrangement contributes. An elementary beginning becomes a measure of an inquiry’s reach. A known conclusion becomes a reason to overlook what another proof explains.

The description has become a verdict. What warrants the passage?

No intellectual life can dispense with abbreviated judgments. Attention is finite, expertise is unevenly distributed, and much of what we learn comes from trusting someone who has already done the work. A useful judgment compresses an examination that others cannot always repeat. The question is what must survive that compression.

## 2. Enough for which question?

Consider [two transformations of the real plane](/#a-reconstruction-example). One leaves every vector unchanged. The other sends \((x,y)\) to \((x+y,y)\). Both have eigenvalues 1 and 1. That information suffices to determine that both have determinant one and are invertible.

It does not determine their behavior under iteration. Starting from \((0,1)\), the first stays at \((0,1)\); the second reaches \((n,1)\) after n applications. The eigenvalue list has forgotten a distinction that matters to this question.

There is no fault in the list for omitting it. Useful descriptions routinely omit information. Their adequacy depends on the inference we want to draw. A richer account can be necessary for one purpose and wasteful for another.

This gives a test: if a description determines an answer, cases it cannot distinguish must agree on that answer. A disagreement identifies a limit of the description. Agreement in a few cases does not establish its general adequacy; that requires an argument that the answer depends only on what the description retains.

A description can also provide evidence for an answer without determining it. Its force then depends on how reliably the retained features bear on the question. The strength of the judgment should reflect what remains uncertain.

“No new theorem” can answer a legitimate question about a paper’s results. It leaves open whether the paper offers a better explanation, a usable procedure, or a connection between existing arguments. Those gains need demonstration. Their presence may justify a place in a textbook while remaining insufficient for a research journal.

## 3. What the arrangement does

A description can preserve individual answers while losing the relationships among them. In topology, recovering the groups assigned to each space leaves a further question: how does a map between spaces act on those groups? The universal coefficient theorem makes this distinction exact. It recovers integral cohomology groups from integral homology through a short exact sequence. The sequence respects maps of spaces—it is natural—and splits as abelian groups. Its splittings cannot in general be chosen to respect those maps.

For example, form \(X\) by attaching an \((n+1)\)-cell to \(S^n\) by a degree-\(m\) map, with \(n\geq1\) and \(m>1\). Collapsing \(S^n\) gives \(q:X\to S^{n+1}\). The reduced cellular chain complex of \(X\) has boundary \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\) in degrees \(n+1\) and \(n\). Its only nonzero reduced integral homology is therefore \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) in degree \(n\). The sphere has reduced homology only in degree \(n+1\), so \(q\) induces zero on reduced homology, just as a constant map \(c\) does.

On top cellular chains, however, \(q\) is the identity. Dualizing gives the identity on top cochains; taking cohomology reduces integers modulo \(m\). In degree \(n+1\), the two pullbacks from \(\mathbb Z\) to \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) satisfy

\[
q^*(1)=1\bmod m,\qquad c^*(1)=0.
\]

The homology maps cannot distinguish these two maps; cohomology does.[^1]

Homology thus determines the cohomology groups up to isomorphism, while its induced maps do not determine the induced cohomology maps. A list of abstract groups can be a complete answer to one question and an inadequate input to the next. Eilenberg and Mac Lane made compatibility with induced maps an explicit object of study.[^2] Recovering each answer and recovering how the answers vary together are different achievements.

This gives “architecture” a demanding meaning. An author has to exhibit a gain: a comparison that becomes available, a hypothesis that can be removed, a dependence that becomes explicit, or a construction that can now be transported. The claim should survive comparison with the strongest existing account relevant to its purpose and readership. A new diagram earns little if an old argument already supplies the same compatibility more clearly.

“The same” therefore needs an object. The same conclusion, the same argument after translation, and the same contribution for a particular use are different comparisons. Two presentations may coincide at one level and diverge at another. A claim of redundancy needs to identify which comparison has actually been made.

A comparison can omit the very information it needs. Broad superiority may be claimed against an unduly weak alternative; prerequisites may be charged to one method while the other’s machinery is treated as free; a favorable example may be detached from the limitation that makes it work. Conversely, an introductory exercise may be taken as the measure of an inquiry while its claimed extension goes unexamined. This is cherry-picking at the level of the comparison: the selection removes what would test the conclusion.

The defect is not selection itself. One counterexample can refute a universal statement, while one favorable example cannot establish general superiority. An account of the surrounding architecture cannot rescue the refuted statement. What matters is whether the selection supports the scope of the claim.

Enough information can still be difficult to use. Two equivalent accounts may differ in how readily a reader can locate a dependence or apply a construction. That explanatory gain must be considered alongside the definitions, translations, and machinery required to use the account.

## 4. What recognition knows

Expertise often makes this comparison almost immediate. A specialist may recognize a theorem under different notation, notice that an alleged extension follows from a standard argument, or locate a fatal counterexample. A brief judgment can contain years of relevant experience. Requiring every assessment to begin from first principles would squander that competence.

Nor is explicit explanation a perfect measure of knowledge. People can recognize a pattern reliably before articulating every cue. Research on intuitive expertise locates its reliability in learnable regularities and opportunities for practice and feedback; felt certainty alone is a poor test.[^3]

Recognizing a false step, recognizing an old theorem, and assessing what a new organization explains are different tasks. Familiarity can guide all three, but success at one does not automatically settle another. “These moves are standard” becomes a strong objection to a claimed conceptual gain when the comparison shows that the gain is standard too.

The author therefore needs a usable entrance: a question, a relevant antecedent, and a worked difference. “You have missed the architecture” is no substitute. A critic who supplies the missing reference may have identified exactly what the author needed to learn. The comparison must be capable of changing what either party claims.

## 5. Reasons for stopping

A reader may reasonably stop because a contribution looks unlikely to repay further attention. A journal may decline a correct paper because other submissions better serve its aims. Such decisions need not wait until every question about the work is settled.

The distinction is between having enough reason to act and having enough reason for a particular assertion. Declining a full review does not establish that a paper has no explanatory value. A relevant antecedent can support a specific claim of redundancy; its force comes from the comparison.

Mathematical publishing guidelines differ on whether editors owe reasons for nonacceptance.[^4] Whenever a substantive reason is given, its scope can remain precise: “The claimed theorem follows from this result under these hypotheses”; or “The comparison is informative, but the journal requires new research results.”

Correcting a claim of redundancy may leave the decision unchanged while withdrawing an unsupported description of the work. The contribution has not been shown absent merely because it was insufficient for that venue.

## 6. Keeping the boundary visible

A useful assessment locates the claim, identifies the comparison, and makes clear how it bears on the purpose. An exact counterexample may suffice; a judgment about explanatory gain may require reconstructing more of the argument.

This makes praise more informative too. A work may deserve attention because it reveals why two constructions agree, makes an obstruction usable, or teaches readers to recognize a mechanism elsewhere. “Conceptual” becomes an account of an achievement rather than a rank assigned to its author.

The original descriptions can then become useful judgments. “Technical” can identify the work still needed. “Elementary” can describe the resources through which an explanation becomes accessible. “A reformulation” can specify an equivalence and allow us to ask what it makes easier to see or do. Sometimes the examination will support “merely.” Sometimes it will reveal the contribution.

Judgment can close an inquiry before everything about a work is known. Its responsibility is to preserve the boundary between what was established, what was judged insufficient for a stated purpose, and what has not been found out.

## Notes and sources

[^1]: Allen Hatcher, [Algebraic Topology](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch3.pdf) (2002), §3.1, Theorem 3.2, pp. 195–196, and exercise 11(a), p. 205. The quotient \(q\) and a constant map agree on all integral homology maps, including degree zero. If the UCT splittings were natural, the induced cohomology map would be determined by the homology maps, contradicting this example. The sequence itself is natural; special cases can split naturally.

[^2]: Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, “[General Theory of Natural Equivalences](https://people.math.osu.edu/cogdell.1/6112-Eilenberg%26MacLane-www.pdf),” Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 58 (1945), 231–294, especially the introduction, pp. 235–236. Their motivation joins conceptual organization with specified mathematical uses, including passage to limits.

[^3]: Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein, “[Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree](https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/kahneman-klein-2009.pdf),” American Psychologist 64 (2009), 515–526, especially pp. 520–524. Their synthesis concerns conditions for intuitive skill and its limits; it supplies no direct measurement of mathematical refereeing.

[^4]: Compare IMU/CEIC, [Best Current Practices for Mathematics Journals](https://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/CEIC/bestpractice/Best_Current_Practices_for_Journals.pdf) (June 2021), §§1.1.1–1.1.2 and 1.3.2, with the appendix to the [AMS Guidelines for Journal Editors](https://www.ams.org/sec-guidelines-jrl-editors). IMU recommends communicating grounds and permits brief editorial justifications; the AMS appendix does not oblige editors to give a rationale for nonacceptance. These recommendations do not settle a universal procedural entitlement.
